concept.name: Reverse Proxy Patterns & Edge Load Balancing

relationships.description: Reverse proxies manage upstream and downstream TCP socket buffers, connections, and keepalive pools.
Reverse proxies can cache static or micro-cached HTTP responses in shared memory to shield backend clusters.
CDNs act as globally distributed reverse proxies terminating traffic close to users via Anycast routing.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Canonical masterclass systems architecture authored with P2C balancing, NGINX/Envoy configurations, and Netflix case study.

spark.summary: A reverse proxy terminates client connections at the network edge, enforces TLS 1.3, rate limits, and auth, and multiplexes requests over persistent upstream pools to backend services using algorithms like Power of Two Choices (P2C) or consistent hashing.
spark.keyTakeaway: Terminate TLS and untrusted client behavior at the proxy boundary so backend services only process normalized, connection-pooled traffic within strict timeout and circuit-breaker budgets.

concept.whyItMatters: Exposing application servers directly to the public internet forces every service to handle slowloris attacks, TLS handshakes, certificate rotation, and heterogeneous HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 framing. A reverse proxy (NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy, Cloudflare Pingora) absorbs connection churn, reduces backend CPU spent on cryptography by 30-50%, and enables zero-downtime routing shifts.
whenToUse: Terminating TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) at the edge while speaking plain HTTP/2 or gRPC over mTLS inside a private VPC.
Consolidating cross-cutting concerns such as JWT validation, token-bucket rate limiting, and gzip/brotli compression in one control plane.
Routing traffic across heterogeneous upstreams using path prefixes, weighted canary splits, or consistent hashing for stateful caches.
whenNotToUse: Ultra-low-latency internal RPCs (<100 microseconds) where an extra L7 hop and buffer copy violates the tail-latency budget.
Raw non-HTTP binary protocols (e.g., custom UDP game state) unless using an L4 passthrough proxy like IPVS or Envoy TCP proxy.
Simple single-binary internal tools behind an existing cloud load balancer where an extra proxy tier adds operational toil without isolation gains.
keyPoints: Connection pooling (keep-alive) between proxy and upstreams eliminates per-request TCP 3-way handshakes and ephemeral port exhaustion.
Power of Two Choices (P2C) with least-requests outperforms round-robin when request latencies vary by >5x across endpoints.
Consistent hashing (Ketama/Maglev) pins keys like user_id or tenant_id to specific upstream shards, preserving local cache hit rates during deploys.
Active health checks plus passive outlier detection (ejecting hosts after 5 consecutive 5xx responses) prevent black-holing traffic to degraded pods.
Buffer tuning (proxy_buffering, max_concurrent_streams) isolates fast backends from slow 3G mobile clients draining responses.

examples.title: API Gateway & Edge Offload at Checkout Scale
examples.scenario: An e-commerce API running 120 Go microservices behind Envoy saw 42% CPU burned on TLS 1.2/1.3 handshakes and 502 spikes during pod autoscaling.
examples.outcome: Enabling Envoy TLS 1.3 session resumption, HTTP/2 upstream connection pools (max_requests_per_connection=10000), and passive outlier detection cut p99 latency from 185 ms to 64 ms and eliminated 502s during scale-in.

examples.title: Stateful Cache Routing with Maglev Hashing
examples.scenario: A distributed feature-store tier of 24 in-memory nodes used round-robin routing, forcing every node to cache the full working set and driving hit rates down to 18%.
examples.outcome: Switching HAProxy to consistent hashing on the entity_id header raised L1 cache hit rates to 91% and dropped p95 read latency from 28 ms to 3.4 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Buffering full request/response bodies protects slow backend workers from being tied up by slow mobile clients.
tradeOffs.con: Increases proxy RAM usage and breaks Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, or large file streaming unless explicitly disabled per route.

tradeOffs.factor: Centralized Edge Proxy vs Sidecar Mesh
tradeOffs.pro: A single edge fleet (NGINX/Envoy) is easy to size, monitor, and upgrade without injecting sidecars into every pod.
tradeOffs.con: Cannot enforce east-west mTLS or per-service circuit breaking between internal microservices without routing hairpins.

tradeOffs.pro: Consistent hashing maximizes upstream cache locality and minimizes key remapping to ~1/N when a node leaves.
tradeOffs.con: Hot keys (celebrity accounts) can overload a single upstream shard regardless of idle capacity on sibling nodes.

failureModes.name: Upstream Keep-Alive Race Condition (502 Bad Gateway)
failureModes.description: The upstream server closes an idle keep-alive connection at the exact millisecond the proxy writes a new request onto that socket, returning HTTP 502.
failureModes.mitigation: Set the proxy's idle connection timeout strictly lower than the upstream server's keepalive_timeout (e.g., 55s in Envoy vs 65s in Gunicorn/Node) and enable safe idempotent retries on connect/reset.

failureModes.name: Proxy Header Spoofing (X-Forwarded-For Injection)
failureModes.description: An attacker sends a forged X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 header, and a misconfigured proxy appends rather than strips untrusted client headers, bypassing IP allowlists.
failureModes.mitigation: Strip or overwrite X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, and Forwarded at the outermost trusted edge proxy, or use PROXY protocol v2 between L4 LB and L7 proxy.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm Amplification
failureModes.description: When an upstream slows down, aggressive proxy retries (3x per hop across 3 service hops) multiply load by 27x, turning a partial brownout into a total outage.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap retry budgets to <=10% of active requests, retry only idempotent methods on connect-failure or 503, and enforce per-route deadlines via x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms.

failureModes.name: Ephemeral Port Exhaustion
failureModes.description: Disabling upstream keep-alive at >20k RPS exhausts the 28k-60k ephemeral TCP ports per proxy IP, leaving sockets stuck in TIME_WAIT.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable HTTP/1.1 keep-alive pools or HTTP/2 multiplexing to upstreams, and bind multiple source IPs or enable tcp_tw_reuse on Linux.

commonMistakes: Leaving proxy_read_timeout at the 60s default while upstream handlers time out at 5s, masking cascading thread exhaustion.
Using round-robin for heterogeneous endpoints where 10ms health pings share workers with 2s PDF exports.
Forgetting to forward Host and X-Forwarded-Proto headers, causing backends to generate broken http:// redirect URLs.
Configuring identical health-check intervals across 50 proxy instances, creating a thundering herd on /healthz.
Treating HTTP 499 (client closed connection) as an upstream server error instead of client-side cancellation.

sections.content:
## The idea

A reverse proxy sits in front of one or more origin servers and acts as the single authoritative network boundary for clients. Unlike a forward proxy (which hides clients from the internet), a reverse proxy hides backend topology from clients—terminating TLS 1.3, normalizing malformed HTTP frames, enforcing rate limits, and multiplexing requests over long-lived upstream pools.

By decoupling client-facing connection lifecycles from backend execution lifecycles, a reverse proxy lets backend services run with small, predictable worker pools (e.g., 16-64 threads) even while serving 100,000+ concurrent slow mobile connections.

## Concrete walkthrough

1. **Edge TLS & ALPN**: A mobile client connects over UDP/443 (HTTP/3 QUIC) or TCP/443 (TLS 1.3). The proxy completes the 1-RTT handshake using session tickets and negotiates `h2` via ALPN.
2. **Header Sanitization & Auth**: The proxy strips untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` headers, appends the verified peer IP, validates a JWT signature against a cached JWKS keyset, and checks a local/Redis token bucket.
3. **Route & Upstream Selection**: Matching `/api/v1/orders/*`, the proxy selects a healthy endpoint from its `orders` cluster using Power of Two Choices (P2C) least-requests.
4. **Pooled Upstream Dispatch**: Rather than opening a new TCP socket, the proxy reuses an idle HTTP/2 stream from its mTLS upstream pool, propagating `traceparent` and setting an `x-request-timeout` deadline of `800ms`.
5. **Response & Outlier Tracking**: The backend returns `200 OK` in `42ms`. If it instead returns `503`, passive outlier detection increments the host's consecutive-error counter and ejects it for `30s` once it hits 5 errors.

sections.content:
## Connection pooling, buffering, and timeouts

Three knobs determine whether a reverse proxy absorbs spikes or amplifies them:

- **Keep-Alive Skew**: Always keep upstream idle timeouts shorter at the proxy (`55s`) than at the application server (`65s`) so the proxy closes idle sockets cleanly instead of racing with a server-side `FIN`.
- **Request/Response Buffering**: Buffering full bodies in proxy memory/disk frees backend worker threads immediately when clients are on slow networks, but must be disabled (`proxy_buffering off`) for SSE, gRPC bi-di streams, and >100 MB downloads.
- **Deadline Propagation**: Forward remaining request budget via `grpc-timeout` or `x-envoy-upstream-rq-timeout-ms` so backends abort work if the client has already timed out.

## Load-balancing algorithms compared

| Algorithm | State Required | Cache Locality | Hot-Key Resilience | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Round-Robin** | O(1) index | None | High | Uniform stateless APIs with identical request cost |
| **Least-Connections / P2C** | Active inflight count | Low | High | Mixed-latency endpoints (10ms reads + 2s exports) |
| **Consistent Hash (Maglev/Ketama)** | Ring / lookup table | Very High (~1/N churn) | Low (needs bounded loads) | In-memory caches, sticky sessions, sharded indexes |
| **Locality-Weighted** | Zone latency + weights | Zone-local | High | Multi-AZ clusters minimizing cross-AZ egress fees |

## Failure modes

- **Retry Amplification**: Unbounded retries across multiple proxy tiers turn a 10% slowdown into a 10x traffic spike. Always enforce a global retry budget (`<=10%` of inflight requests) and never retry non-idempotent `POST` calls on `504`.
- **Head-of-Line Blocking on HTTP/2 Upstreams**: Multiplexing 1,000 requests onto a single TCP connection means one lost packet stalls all 1,000 streams. Cap `max_concurrent_streams` per upstream connection (e.g., `100`) and maintain multiple pooled TCP connections per host.
- **DNS Stale Caching**: NGINX OSS caches upstream DNS at startup unless configured with `resolver` and `valid=10s` inside a variable-based `proxy_pass`, causing 502s after cloud ALB IP rotations.

## Observability and graceful draining

Separate proxy-originated errors from upstream errors in metrics and access logs:

- Log both `upstream_status` and `status`, plus `upstream_connect_time`, `upstream_header_time`, and `upstream_response_time`.
- During proxy upgrades or scale-in, stop accepting new connections (fail `/readyz`), send HTTP/2 `GOAWAY` frames on existing client connections, and wait `drain_timeout` (e.g., `30s`) before closing sockets.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Strip and re-set `X-Forwarded-For` / `Forwarded` at the outermost trusted edge proxy.
- [ ] Set proxy upstream idle keep-alive timeout 10s lower than the backend server's timeout.
- [ ] Enable P2C least-requests for variable-latency APIs; reserve consistent hashing for stateful caches.
- [ ] Cap retry budgets at <=10% of active traffic and restrict retries to idempotent methods on connect/503 errors.
- [ ] Configure passive outlier detection (5 consecutive 5xx -> 30s ejection) alongside jittered active health checks.
- [ ] Set explicit connect (`2s`), header (`15s`), and total request timeouts, and disable buffering on SSE/streaming routes.

questions.title: Upstream Keepalive Connection Pooling
questions.prompt: Why is configuring 'proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection "";' critical when configuring an NGINX reverse proxy to route to backend clusters?

options.text: By default, NGINX uses HTTP/1.0 with 'Connection: close' for upstreams; clearing the header and using HTTP/1.1 allows persistent socket reuse from the upstream keepalive pool.
options.explanation: Correct! Without these directives, NGINX closes the backend TCP socket after every single request, causing high CPU consumption from repeated handshakes and ephemeral port exhaustion.

options.text: It encrypts the payload using AES-256 before transmitting over the internal network.
options.explanation: HTTP version and Connection headers do not handle symmetric payload encryption.

options.text: It disables all HTTP caching on the proxy.
options.explanation: Upstream connection headers regulate transport socket reuse, not caching headers like Cache-Control.

options.text: It bypasses the proxy event loop and streams directly to disk.
options.explanation: It enables socket reuse within the event loop.

rubric.excellent: Identifies default HTTP/1.0 behavior and explains how keepalive connection pools eliminate handshake overhead.
rubric.gap: Confuses connection headers with encryption or caching.

questions.sampleSolution: By default, NGINX forwards requests using HTTP/1.0 with Connection: close, destroying the TCP socket; clearing the header enables persistent keepalive pool reuse.
questions.explanation: Always enable HTTP/1.1 and clear the Connection header for upstreams in NGINX.

interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design an edge reverse proxy tier handling 50,000 requests per second across 50 distinct microservices. How do you handle routing, TLS termination, backend health checking, and prevent noisy neighbors from crashing the tier?
constraints: Must isolate slow backend services from consuming all proxy worker threads
Must support automated canary deployments with weighted traffic shifting
Must achieve sub-3ms p99 proxy overhead

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use Envoy proxy with P2C load balancing, configure isolated connection pools and circuit breakers per upstream cluster, terminate TLS at the edge with session tickets, and enforce token bucket rate limits per tenant.
commonPitfalls: Sharing a global unbounded connection pool across all microservices.
